title: Design tokens — Image Wiki
text:
Design tokens
  A named decision. The point of calling a colour color.text.default rather than #1B1B1B is that the name can be pointed somewhere else once, for everybody.

  
    Termdesign token / design system
    Also calledtokens, style variables, theme values, design decisions
    Not the same astoken vs value, design system vs style guide, theme vs brand
    Read7 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        A token is a name, not a valueThe layersThe trade-offCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Next time you are on a road in the United States, look at a route shield: a white shield outline with black numerals. Nobody who fabricated the one you are looking at chose that. It was settled in 1927 by a committee, written down, and copied ever since.
That is what a design system is once you strip the enthusiasm off it: a set of decisions made once, given names, and applied by people who will never meet whoever made them. Everything else — the component library, the Figma file, the documentation site — is machinery for delivering those decisions to strangers.


Specified: 1927
Built: Georgia, 2013


Left: Plate II of the AASHO Manual and Specifications for U.S. Standard Road Markers and Signs, 1927 (public domain). Right: a signpost in Georgia, photographed in 2013 by Dougtone (CC BY-SA 2.0).
Left, four designs, each with a code printed under it: M-4 the small directional shield, M-19 the arrow, M-19A the double arrow, D-4 the junction plate. The accompanying text is a specification, not advice: the route marker "is a shield bearing the name of the State, the number of the route and the letters 'U.S.'", and "the background color of the shield is white and the design black" (AASHO-1927).
Right, eighty-six years later, on a roadside in Georgia. The shield, the black-on-white scheme and the plain arrow plaque are all still there, on a post assembled by somebody who never read the manual. The decision outlived the committee, the drawing and the technology — which is the only test of a system that matters.


A token is a name, not a value
USWDS states the problem better than most software documentation. CSS will accept almost anything: there are over 16 million colours in RGB, and font size, line height and spacing take a similarly wide range. "This degree of choice can slow down design work and make communication between designer and developer unnecessarily granular" (SYS-002). Their answer is a curated shortlist — "just like a scale of musical notes is drawn from the spectrum of all possible frequencies. Or like the presets on a car radio."
Their measure token is the cleanest example. Line length could be any number in em, rem, ch, ex or px to two decimal places. USWDS ships seven values, and that is all: 44ex, 60ex, 64ex, 68ex, 72ex, 88ex, and none (SYS-002).
Atlassian defines a token as "name and value pairings that represent small, repeatable design decisions", and gives the reason a name beats a value: instead of choosing one of many shades of green for an icon, you apply color.icon.success (SYS-012). The green is not the decision. Which green means success is the decision, and it now has an address.

componentsraw valueButtonCardTable header#1B1B1B#1B1B1B#1B1B1Bthree copiesto keep in stepa new text colour means three edits, found by grepValue written into each componentthe decision exists three times and is named nowherecomponentstoken nameraw valueButtonCardTable headercolor.text.default#1B1B1Ba new text colour means one edit, in one fileValue behind a namethe decision exists once and has an address

The mechanism, and it is not complicated. Left, three components with the hex written into each. The decision exists three times, is named nowhere, and can only be found by searching for the string.
Right, the same three ask for color.text.default, and the value sits behind the name. Changing the text colour of the product is now one edit. USWDS is strict about this and puts it in bold in their own docs: "We do not include the token's value directly into our Sass rules" — components call a function, mixin or utility class instead (SYS-002).


The 1927 manual worked the same way. The shield is design M-3; the dimensions live on a separate sheet, working drawing M-1. Fabricators are told the code and sent to the drawing. Change the drawing, and every future sign changes.



Plate XXI, Caution Series, AASHO 1927. Public domain.
This is what "a limited set of discrete options" looks like on paper. Six diamonds, and every one has a number: C-1 is HILL, C-2 is HILL SHIFT GEAR, C-3 is CURVE, and so on. A county engineer does not design a warning sign. They pick one, by number, from a list.
The list is also revealing about what a system is for. When a state needed something new, the manual says the design would be worked out with them and "thereafter be included in the list, and any other State wishing a sign for the same purpose will find it provided among the Standards" (AASHO-1927). A contribution process, in 1927, in one sentence.


The layers
Names sit in a stack, and the stack is the part people get wrong.
At the bottom is the raw value: #1B1B1B, 16px, 240ms. It carries no meaning at all. Above it sits the semantic name that says what the value is for — Atlassian's grammar is foundation, then property, then an optional modifier, so color.text is the default body text colour and the modifier narrows it from there (SYS-012). At the top is usage: a component reaches for the semantic name and never touches the raw value.
The middle layer is the one that earns its keep, because it is what makes a theme possible. A theme is just "a collection of token values designed to achieve a certain look or style" — light mode, dark mode and high-contrast mode are all themes, and Atlassian points out that non-colour themes work the same way: compact views, reduced motion, custom typography (SYS-012).

Card titleContinuecolor.text.default#1B1B1Bcolor.background.default#FFFFFFcolor.border#E2E5EAthe card asks for the three names on the rightand never mentions a colourLight themeone set of values behind the namesCard titleContinuecolor.text.default#E8EAEEcolor.background.default#14161Acolor.border#2B2F37the card is the same file, unchangedonly the values movedDark themeanother set of values behind the same names

The same card, twice. It asks for color.text.default, color.background.default and color.border, and the component file is byte-for-byte identical in both panels. Only the values behind the three names moved.
This is also where the sharpest practical rule in the whole subject comes from. Atlassian's "don't" is: "Don't use a token just because the colors appear to match. This can break the experience in other themes" (SYS-012). A border token that happens to be the same grey as your divider today will diverge the moment somebody builds high-contrast mode.


The trade-off
A system buys two things: consistency across work nobody coordinated, and speed, because most decisions are already made. USWDS's design principles put the second one first — the system exists so teams can "start with real user needs" rather than re-deciding grey (SYS-001-C01).
It costs flexibility, and pretending otherwise is how systems get abandoned. So the real question is not should we have tokens but which decisions deserve to be frozen. The answer that holds up: freeze the decisions where variation carries no information — the exact grey of a border, the gap under a heading, the duration of a fade — and leave free the decisions where variation is the point.
Mature systems also ship escape hatches, deliberately. GOV.UK provides override classes like govuk-!-margin-9 for "minor adjustments" (SYS-008). USWDS exposes nine theme font-size tokens drawn from a deeper set of twenty-one system tokens, and tells you to reach into the larger set if nine is genuinely not enough (SYS-002). An override you can name is much better than a hard-coded value nobody can find.
The governance argument is identical to the one in Identity systems, which makes it about a 1976 paper binder rather than a Sass file. Nothing important changed in fifty years except the file format.
Common mistakes

"Tokens are variables." Variables hold values. Tokens hold decisions, which is why their names describe use (color.text.default) and not appearance (dark-grey). A token called blue cannot survive a rebrand.
"More tokens means more consistency." The opposite. USWDS's seven measure values are useful because there are seven. A palette of two hundred tokens is a continuum with extra steps.
"The design system is the component library." The components are downstream. The system is the set of frozen decisions plus the machinery — and the governance — that gets them to people you will never meet.
"We will name things properly later." Naming is the deliverable. #1B1B1B in three files is not three-quarters of a token.


Reading a system in five steps

Pick one visible property — a grey, a gap, a corner radius. Does it have a name?
Does the name say what it is for, or what it looks like?
How many values exist for that property? If the answer is "as many as we needed", there is no scale.
Change one token in your head. How many screens move? If the answer is one, the indirection is fake.
Find the escape hatch. A system with no sanctioned override has an unsanctioned one.



  
    
      Read next
      
        
          
            
              Type scales and spacing scales
              The two most-used scales in any design system — a short list of text sizes and a short list of gaps. Both work only if adjacent steps are far enough apart to look deliberate.
            
          
        
          
            
              Identity systems
              The set of decisions that make a mark work everywhere — colour, typeface, grid, formats, signage, artwork masters and the rules about who may change what. Its real purpose is governance, not beauty.
            
          
        
          
            
              Logo reproduction tests
              The set of physical conditions a mark has to survive — one colour, small size, reversed on dark, blurred, stitched, next to competitors — and the mechanism that makes each one fail.
            
          
        
          
            
              Grids
              A set of decisions taken once — margins, columns, gutters, modules, baselines — so that no later page needs a fresh decision. It is a system, not a look.
